unit.title: You become what you practice
unit.needIt: Nobody decides to be patient or brave. You do the patient thing, clumsily, many times, and one day it is just how you are.
unit.why: Aristotle believed we become good by doing good things until they become automatic. The lecture explains how we can use science to turn our goals into these automatic habits.
unit.outcome: Create a plan to turn a goal into a daily habit using rewards and environment changes.
unit.reachesYou: You see this when you struggle to stop checking your phone or when you find it hard to start a new workout. It shows up every time you try to change a small daily routine.
unit.do: Identify one bad habit and remove the tool that makes it easy, like putting your phone in another room.

choices: A rule of how things should be
quiz.why: Normative laws are about 'oughts' or how people should behave.
quiz.quote: They are laws in the sense that you find over at the Yale law school. But in addition, there are laws of a very different kind spread around the rest of campus. Spread around, in fact, everything that you ever do. And those are descriptive laws.

choices: A fact about how the world is
quiz.why: Descriptive laws describe how things actually behave in the world.
quiz.quote: They tell you the way things actually are. So it would be sort of funny to have a t-shirt, if a car hits you, you will die. It's not just a bad thing. It's the law.

quiz.q: How does Aristotle say we learn a craft?
quiz.why: Aristotle argues that we learn by doing the action itself.
quiz.quote: So when Aristotle says we learn a craft by producing the same product that we must produce when we've learned it, we become builders by building, harpists by playing the harp in the same way, we become just by doing just

quiz.q: What happens to behaviors that are initially under conscious control?
quiz.why: Repeated practice turns conscious actions into automatic routines.
quiz.quote: So patterns of behavior that are initially under conscious control can, through a process of repeated practice, become automatized.

quiz.q: What is a neutral stimulus in classical conditioning?
quiz.why: A neutral stimulus is something that initially produces no specific response.
quiz.quote: By contrast, there are lots of things in the world, bells for example, which produce in the dog no reaction at all. You ring a bell, the dog goes, big woof. Who cares, it's a bell.

quiz.q: What is operant conditioning concerned with?
quiz.why: Operant conditioning looks at how behaviors are shaped by their consequences.
quiz.quote: Operant conditioning is concerned with the relation between behaviors that you yourself perform and the outcomes to which those behaviors typically give rise.

quiz.why: Negative reinforcement increases a behavior by taking away something unpleasant.
quiz.quote: I can provide you with positive reinforcement for desired behavior, or one can reinforce a desired behavior through what is technically known as negative reinforcement, the removal of an aversive stimulus.

decoys.why: Aristotle says arguments alone are not sufficient to make people decent.
